interval.label: Selected mill, training, storage and legal changes, 1872–1916
interval.note: A selected source frame from Tomioka’s opening to Factory Act implementation, extending four years beyond the Meiji period. It is not the mill’s operating lifespan or the beginning/end of Japanese industrialization. The earlier 1863 farmhouse and a later 1917 worker recollection are explicitly contextual comparisons. The original exact October 1872 case remains unchanged. Memoir writing/publication, modern scholarship, heritage listing and digitization have separate dates.

sourcesToConsult.title: Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites
sourcesToConsult.scope: Prior consultation, 2026-10-26 (retained): Integrated production, local sericultural traditions and imported/adapted technology. Tomioka selected consultation, 2026-10-29: Brief synthesis, criteria and selected integrity/authenticity paragraphs read on 29 October. Use is limited to differentiated sericulture/reeling functions, adaptation and distinct component histories; the criterion’s wholly successful-transfer language is not adopted as proof of every worker’s welfare. 2014 is inscription, not the creation date of every site. Historic management statements are not renewed 2026 enforcement claims. No full nomination, source plan or photograph inspected/reused; direct local capture returned 403 but the selected web text was readable.

sourcesToConsult.title: Arafune Cold Storage
sourcesToConsult.institution: Japan Tourism Agency, JTA Sightseeing Database; associated board Gunma Prefecture
sourcesToConsult.published: FY 2020 prepared; exact publication day unstated
sourcesToConsult.scope: FY Prepared metadata and complete exposed English interpretation read, especially Preparing for storage. First units operated in 1905; three existed by 1914. The text describes cooled storage, marked egg cards, testing, labels/cataloguing and returning cards when needed. Its current visitor interpretation is not an original 1905 inventory or measured historical temperature series. The absolute summer-temperature claim, exact total capacity and possible prehistoric cold-storage use are not adopted. No building reconstruction, transport route, photograph, source geometry or source image copied. Linked English PDF/Word files were not read.

sourcesToConsult.title: March 1911: the Factory Act is established (工場法が成立する)
sourcesToConsult.institution: National Archives of Japan, Japan’s Progress digital exhibition
sourcesToConsult.scope: Short Japanese institutional explanatory paragraph, title, cabinet-file identifier 類01128 and displayed links read. Editorial English paraphrase: promulgation 28 March 1911, protective provisions and initial factory-size scope, implementation September 1916. No full original statute, cabinet file, imperial signed original, page-image transcription or current legal guidance consulted. The institutional caption distinguishes enactment from implementation; it does not prove compliance at any selected factory. The page’s publication date is unstated; its footer copyright is not a publication date. No source image reused.

sourcesToConsult.title: The Training and Education of Female Silk-reeling Instructors in Meiji Japan
sourcesToConsult.author: Sashinami Akiko
sourcesToConsult.institution: Accessing Technical Education in Modern Japan, chapter 10, pp. 252–278; Amsterdam University Press
sourcesToConsult.scope: Exposed Summary/Introduction paragraphs and chapter/author/publisher/pages/DOI metadata read. Print year 2022; displayed online date 26 May 2022. DOI 10.1017/9781912961269.012. Selected text describes sorting cocoons, drawing and joining filaments, reeling at machine speed and women teaching other women. The full chapter, its figure 1, original training records and linked translation notes were not consulted. The broad historical gender allocation is not adopted as universal household practice. No source image, machine geometry or modern replication copied; no figure reuse licence established.

sourcesToConsult.title: Silk-reeling Technology and Female Labour
sourcesToConsult.author: Masanori Nakamura; Corrado Molteni
sourcesToConsult.institution: Technology Change and Female Labour in Japan, chapter 1; United Nations University Press; hosted by IDE/JETRO
sourcesToConsult.scope: Selected opening/process framing; Tomioka recruitment and Rokkūsha/Nakayamasha adaptation passages; selected Suwa working-hours, Factory Act exceptions, 1917 applications and Okaya recollection; and notes 11, 41–45 read in the institutional English HTML. The opening process sequence is explicitly about c.1910–1920s and is not redated to 1872. Wada is named Hide in this chapter; the separately consulted NDL record uses Ei(ko). Her recollection is mediated through the authors and their cited 1978 edition, pp. 21–22. The unnamed Okaya worker’s 1917 experience is mediated through a 1981 publication cited at note 45, p. 56; the authors cite a 1919 annual reporting on 1917 at note 44. No original Japanese memoir, 1903 survey, legislation, inspection annual, 1981 interview volume or full underlying tables inspected. No complete book/PDF, image, plan or machine diagram consulted/copied. Suwa and Matsushiro evidence is not a Tomioka payroll or universal factory history.

sourcesToConsult.title: Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites
sourcesToConsult.scope: Prior consultation, 2026-10-26 (retained): Government mill opened October 1872; Japanese carpenters and French design; silk-producing region and training. Tomioka selected consultation, 2026-10-29: Selected English Tomioka/Women Mill Workers/Farmhouses/Cold Storage text read on 29 October: local building skills and October 1872 opening, trainers/dormitories, 1863 Tajima farmhouse ventilation, 1884 Takayama-sha school and egg-storage functions. Institutional claims about recruitment and women’s bodies are not adopted as universal experience or biological fact. No original worker records or payroll read. Current residency, universal temperature limits and blanket improved-life claims are not renewed. No source image or geometry copied; the living page has no stated publication date.

sourcesToConsult.title: Tomioka Silk Mill and Related Sites: geographical data
sourcesToConsult.scope: Actual four-row current Geographical data table read: IDs 1449-001 through 1449-004, named components and north/east degrees/minutes/seconds. These are published modern property-reference points to the displayed second, not exact historical workstations, boundaries, routes or origins of all cocoons. Current Tajima coordinates N36 14 48/E139 14 21 differ by one second each from the older nomination table exposed in search; no survey correction inferred. No source map or nomination plan copied/traced. The linked 2014 inscribed-property map and 249 MB nomination were not read. Direct local capture returned 403; this consultation used the readable web response.

sourcesToConsult.title: Construction of large scale government operated factories: Tomioka and Wada Ei(ko)
sourcesToConsult.institution: National Diet Library, Modern Japan and France digital exhibition
sourcesToConsult.scope: Selected Tomioka subsection, Wada biographical paragraph and displayed bibliographic entries read. Wada joined in April 1873, left in July 1874, taught at Saijō/Rokkōsha and became a prefectural-mill instructor in 1878. NDL states that she wrote memories from 1907 onward and records their edited 1931 publication as Tomioka Kōki/Tomioka Nikki. The original Japanese memoir and 1931/1978 editions were not read or independently translated. The linked old OPAC endpoint failed after redirect; it was not retried. Other industries/chapters are outside this renewal. The web page’s publication date is unstated; 1931 is the memoir edition’s date. The NDL brackets the selected Kuniteru print as [1872]. No claim of direct, contemporary diary access or a representative account of every worker.

sourcesToConsult.title: Ghana: A Country Study
sourcesToConsult.institution: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress
sourcesToConsult.scope: LaVerle Berry, editor, 1995. Historical Setting, printed pp. 26–36 (PDF pp. 70–80), consulted for organizing, regional opposition, constitutional change and repression. Later US government synthesis with dated terminology and interpretive judgments; used alongside Ghanaian institutions and primary records. No unqualified “first independent African country” claim is adopted.
sourcesToConsult.author: LaVerle Berry, editor

sourcesToConsult.title: 70 jaar soevereiniteitsoverdracht aan Indonesië
sourcesToConsult.scope: Full account consulted for the 27 December 1949 federal transfer and explicit exclusion of Netherlands New Guinea. No modern territorial boundary is reconstructed.

sourcesToConsult.title: Naskah Sumber Arsip Presiden RI: Sukarno
sourcesToConsult.scope: 2015 archival volume: indexed description identifies Sukarno’s handwritten proclamation draft on printed p. 7 (PDF p. 13), ANRI Teks Proklamasi I. Description and attribution consulted through the web PDF; direct download returned 403 and the screenshot service did not return viewable pixels. The separately credited typed facsimile was visually inspected. This volume is not used as a general biography or a complete history of the revolution.

sourcesToConsult.title: Proklamasi.png: typed proclamation facsimile
sourcesToConsult.scope: File page and actual 399 × 268 image inspected. Typed facsimile with Sukarno/Hatta signatures; different from the handwritten ANRI draft. Record asserts Indonesian government-work public-domain status. The digital upload date is not the document date. Low-resolution copy; no invented restoration.

sourcesToConsult.title: Soevereiniteitsoverdracht Indonesië, 1949
sourcesToConsult.scope: Full Dutch archival teaching page consulted: 1945 proclamation, disputed sovereignty, negotiations, federal settlement and 27 December 1949 transfer. The archive’s transfer vocabulary describes the Dutch legal act; it does not replace Indonesia’s 1945 proclamation date. Exact Linggajati signing day is not adopted from this summary.

sourcesToConsult.title: 1945–1949: Van Nederlands-Indië naar Indonesië
sourcesToConsult.scope: Full Dutch military-history timeline consulted, especially 1945, July 1947, December 1948, May/December 1949 and 1950. An institutional account of Dutch operations and diplomacy, not a survey of Indonesian civilian experiences. Colonial euphemisms are identified rather than used as neutral labels.

sourcesToConsult.title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi original documents: selected sheets and signatures
sourcesToConsult.institution: Archives New Zealand, Te Rua Mahara o te Kāwanatanga
sourcesToConsult.scope: Selected English introduction and sheet 1 Waitangi, sheet 3 Waikato-Manukau, sheet 4 Printed and sheet 7 Herald-Bunbury descriptions read, plus the sheet 2 final-signing paragraph. The Māori counterpart text was exposed but was not independently translated or line-collated. Sheet 3 initial signing date is unknown; late March/early April receipt, 11 April witnessing and 26 April Manukau signing are distinct. Āwhitu is a likely location, not a verified precise spot. Selected southward signings and Nohorua’s request for a witness were read in this institutional account, not the original voyage journal. The Waimate date and initial Waitangi signature counts differ from other institutional pages; no exact disputed count/date adopted. All nine sheet images and signature biographies were not read. No source map, image, route or border copied. Page publication date unstated; item-specific Flickr rights and dated-image metadata are separately recorded, not assumed covered by a generic website licence.

sourcesToConsult.title: Kāwanatanga – Māori engagement with the state: selected pages 1–3
sourcesToConsult.author: Paul Meredith; Rawinia Higgins
sourcesToConsult.institution: Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand; Manatū Taonga
sourcesToConsult.scope: Actual pages 1 Defining kāwanatanga, 2 Implementing kāwanatanga and 3 Containing Māori opposition text and displayed footnotes read; story footer gives published 20 October 2015, updated 1 August 2016. An associated photo caption carries a different story-publication metadata date; no image borrowed. Selected explanation of terms, early limits of colonial administration, 1844 Native Exemption Ordinance, armed enforcement and later institutions provides attributed Māori scholarship. The full page 4, original ordinances/newspapers, 1976 facsimile volume, 1989 Kawharu book and cited tribunal report were not read. The source’s shorthand English wording is not substituted for the separately consulted complete English treaty transcription. No universal Māori interpretation or current legal guidance claimed. Text marked CC BY-NC 4.0; all non-text subject to separate conditions, no figures/maps reused.

sourcesToConsult.title: Justin Tipa: Hui Whakaū I Te Tiriti ki Ōnuku Waitangi Day 2025 commemoration speech
sourcesToConsult.author: Justin Tipa
sourcesToConsult.scope: Header/date and selected transcript passages on Ōnuku/Iwikau/Tīkao, Ngāi Tahu experience, rangatiratanga, constitutional monarchy and collective versus individual rights read. The posted text is a named 2025 political/commemorative perspective, not a contemporary 1840 transcript or universal Māori position. Tipa’s role is described as at that speech; current 2026 office not checked. Video was not played, full audio was not independently transcribed and Ngāi Tahu’s broader positions were not audited. References to contemporary bills, court proceedings and outcomes were not updated or adopted as current facts. No image reused; no broad endorsement/assent inferred.

sourcesToConsult.title: Ōnuku Rūnanga: home and Treaty place
sourcesToConsult.scope: Selected welcome, Ōnuku Rūnanga self-description and historical-place paragraph read. The community identifies the 30 May 1840 signing within the Ngāi Tahu takiwā and the 1998 Crown apology there. The page is undated; no footer year used as publication date. Current marae self-description is not an 1840 building plan, surveyed signing spot or statement for all iwi. The underlying settlement statute, original signing journal, linked gallery, tours and full local history were not read. No photograph, contact detail or source geometry copied. Permission for image reuse not established.

sourcesToConsult.title: The Treaty of Waitangi trail: 21 May proclamation transcript and circulation
sourcesToConsult.institution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa; Treaty2U partnership
sourcesToConsult.scope: Complete exposed proclamation transcript and selected signing/refusal/circulation narrative read. Transcript is the published 21 May 1840 proclamation asserting sovereignty over all the islands; it is not a record of every rangatira consenting. The source’s latitude wording is not adopted as geographic-coordinate evidence. Primary proclamation image is credited to Alexander Turnbull Library, 1/2-081956-F; linked catalogue reader exposed no usable record body, and pixels were not inspected/reused. The gifts bill was exposed as a mediated transcript, not independently checked against the original; no quantitative inference adopted. Treaty2U content originally 2008, reviewed 2020. No current constitutional/legal-status opinion or complete voyage history claimed.

sourcesToConsult.title: Treaty signatories and signing locations: selected record guidance and northern signings
sourcesToConsult.institution: Manatū Taonga, Ministry for Culture and Heritage, NZHistory
sourcesToConsult.scope: Introduction to the nine sheets/1877 facsimile numbering and selected linked Waitangi 6 February, Mangungu 12 February and Te Wherowhero biography text read. Related URLs: /politics/treaty/location/waitangi/6-february-1840; /politics/treaty/location/mangungu/12-february-1840; /politics/declaration/signatory/te-wherowhero. Lists preserve uncertain names and later researched affiliations; facsimile numbers are not necessarily signing order. Nene/Heke support at Waitangi, disagreement at Mangungu and Te Wherowhero’s refusal/continued engagement are attributed institutional accounts. Original journals, speeches, full biographies’ cited scholarship and the 1877 volume were not freshly read. No complete database, signatory total or survey coordinate verification claimed. Text licence displayed CC BY-NC 3.0 New Zealand; no image reuse proposed. Publication day unstated on consulted pages.

sourcesToConsult.title: Report on Stage 1 of the Te Paparahi o Te Raki Inquiry Released
sourcesToConsult.scope: Complete official release and question-and-answer text read, not the full two-part report or evidentiary record. The finding concerns meaning/effect for February 1840 signings at Waitangi, Waimate and Mangungu in the Bay of Islands/Hokianga, not every district or later signing. The release concludes those rangatira did not cede sovereignty and agreed to distinct spheres of authority; it expressly does not determine how/when the Crown acquired present sovereignty or the Treaty’s present meaning. Waimate dated 10 February and Waitangi count 43–46 differ from Archives’ 9 February/42–45. Those discrepancies are recorded; no census-like total or invented reconciliation. Modern finding date is separate from 1840 events. No court/tribunal record update beyond this historical release claimed.

sourcesToConsult.title: Tribunal releases report on Te Paparahi o Te Raki inquiry
sourcesToConsult.scope: Complete exposed official release read. It describes the pre-publication part 1 stage 2 report on Te Raki interactions 1840–1900. Adopted reading is limited to attributed findings about May proclamations, unclear explanation of sole Crown authority, Northern War 1844–46 and imposed land/governance processes. The full report, hearing evidence, later final edition, individual claims, recommendations and present implementation were not read/renewed. No unqualified national extrapolation, exact land-loss statistic, current deprivation measure or completed-redress claim adopted. Stage 1 and stage 2 answer different questions; modern publication date is not a historical phase date.

sourcesToConsult.title: The full text of Te Tiriti o Waitangi | The Treaty of Waitangi
sourcesToConsult.institution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa; Treaty2U partnership with Archives New Zealand and the National Library
sourcesToConsult.scope: Complete exposed Māori transcription, original English transcription and separate modern Kawharu English translation read, including preambles, articles 1–3 and closing formulas. Te Papa attributes the transcriptions to handwritten originals, Archives reference IA9/9; no independent palaeographic verification of all original sheets/signatures. It distinguishes the English Waikato-Manukau signing text from the Māori text signed at Waitangi. Web content originated in Treaty2U in 2008 and was reviewed in 2020; these are not document dates. Te Papa attributes its Kawharu translation to the 1988 Royal Commission on Social Policy report; the underlying volume was not read. Other institutions give differing modern translation/bibliography dates, recorded separately rather than silently reconciled. No full document or image reproduced; selected terms and attributed paraphrases only. No new translation made.

sourcesToConsult.title: Māori and English texts: statutory transcriptions and Kawharu commentary
sourcesToConsult.author: I. H. Kawharu (modern translation and commentary); Waitangi Tribunal (published text editions)
sourcesToConsult.scope: Complete exposed English and Māori text editions, separate modern English translation and all eleven commentary notes read. The site identifies the first two as taken from the first schedule to the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, not newly transcribed directly from all 1840 sheets. Kawharu’s commentary is an attributed scholarly interpretation, including the article 3 tikanga problem; it is not a statement from every signatory. The page’s reference combines a 1989 date with Waitangi Revisited and its later editor set; no original book was read to establish or correct that bibliography. Archives separately labels a translation 1975 and Te Papa cites a 1988 report. A living webpage publication date and the translation’s first composition date remain unestablished. No current legislation/jurisprudence comparison, full text reproduction, independent translation or image reuse claimed.

sourcesToConsult.title: The Treaty of Waitangi and how it happened
sourcesToConsult.scope: Prior consultation (2026-10-26) retained: 6 February 1840 initial signing, circulating sheets, signatures and refusals; not universal consent on one day. Selected 29 October 2026 Tiriti renewal: Selected English sections on drafting, 5–6 February discussion/signing, circulating copies, early September endpoint, refusals/uneven opportunity and 21 May sovereignty proclamations read on 29 October. Original Māori paragraph bodies were exposed but not independently translated. No full journals, all signature biographies, complete nine-sheet palaeography or source images inspected. British assertions are identified as claims of authority, not proof of universal assent. Prior 26 October scope remains separately retained.

sourcesToConsult.title: What te Tiriti o Waitangi says in English and te reo Māori
sourcesToConsult.scope: Prior consultation (2026-10-26) retained: Paired texts and explanation of article 1 governance/sovereignty and article 2 authority/property differences. Selected 29 October 2026 Tiriti renewal: Selected English explanation plus complete exposed original English transcription and separately headed Kawharu modern English back-translation read on 29 October. The current page does not expose a complete original signed Māori transcription; that was read separately at Te Papa. Its modern back-translation heading says 1975, whereas Te Papa attributes its version to 1988 and the Tribunal page gives a 1989/bibliography combination. No first-creation date for Kawharu’s translation or silent correction inferred. Articles 1 and 2 remain compared in context; this renewal does not claim an independent Māori translation or current legal adjudication. Complete prior 26 October scope retained.
